title: Amelia Earhart
wiki_lead:
Amelia Mary Earhart ( AIR-hart; born July 24, 1897; disappeared July 2, 1937; declared dead January 5, 1939) was an American aviator who became one of the most celebrated aviation pioneers.  
In 1928, Earhart was the first woman to cross the Atlantic by airplane. In 1932, she became the first woman to make a nonstop solo transatlantic flight, and was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for her achievement. She was one of the first aviators to promote commercial air travel, wrote best-selling books about her flying experiences, and helped found the Ninety-Nines, an organization for women pilots.

On July 2, 1937, Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan disappeared over the Pacific Ocean in a twin-engine Lockheed Model 10 Electra while attempting to become the first female pilot to circumnavigate the world. Since her disappearance, Earhart has become a global cultural figure and numerous films, documentaries, and books have recounted her life.

Early life


Childhood

Amelia Mary Earhart was born on July 24, 1897, in Atchison, Kansas, the daughter of Samuel "Edwin" Stanton Earhart (1867–1930) and Amelia "Amy" Earhart (née Otis; 1869–1962). She was born in the home of her maternal grandfather Alfred Gideon Otis (1827–1912), who was a former judge in Kansas, the president of Atchison Savings Bank, and a leading resident of the town. Earhart was the second child of the marriage after a stillbirth in August 1896. She was of part German descent. Alfred had not initially favored the marriage and was not satisfied with Edwin's progress as a lawyer.
Following family custom, Earhart was named after her two grandmothers, Amelia Josephine Harres and Mary Wells Patton. From an early age, she was the dominant sibling, while her sister Grace Muriel Earhart (1899–1998), two years her junior, acted as a dutiful follower. Earhart was nicknamed "Meeley" and sometimes "Millie", and Grace was nicknamed "Pidge." Both continued to answer to their childhood nicknames into adulthood. Their upbringing was unconventional; Amy did not believe in raising her children to be "nice little girls". Their maternal grandmother disapproved of the bloomers they wore, and although Earhart liked the freedom of movement they provided, she was aware that the neighborhood girls wore dresses.

The Earhart children had a spirit of adventure and explored their neighborhood daily. As a child, Earhart spent hours playing with Pidge, climbing trees, hunting rats with a rifle, and sledding downhill. Some biographers have characterized her as a tomboy. The girls kept worms, moths, katydids, and a tree toad in a growing collection. In 1904, with the help of her uncle, Earhart constructed a homemade ramp modeled after a roller coaster she had seen on a trip to St. Louis, Missouri, and secured it to the roof of the family tool shed. After her first documented "flight", she emerged from the broken wooden box that had served as a sled with a bruised lip, a torn dress, and a "sensation of exhilaration", saying, "Oh, Pidge, it's just like flying!"
In 1907, Edwin's job as a claims officer for the Rock Island Railroad led to a transfer to Des Moines, Iowa. The following year, at the age of 10, Earhart saw her first aircraft at the Iowa State Fair in Des Moines. Her father tried to interest his daughters in taking a flight, but after looking at the rickety "flivver", Earhart asked if they could return to the merry‑go‑round. She later described the biplane as "a thing of rusty wire and wood and not at all interesting".


Education
Earhart and her sister remained with their grandparents in Atchison while their parents moved into new, smaller quarters in Des Moines. During this period, the girls received homeschooling from their mother and a governess. Earhart later said she was "exceedingly fond of reading" and spent many hours in the large family library. grok_lead: Amelia Mary Earhart (born July 24, 1897, Atchison, Kansas â disappeared July 2, 1937) was an American aviator renowned for setting multiple aviation records and becoming the first woman to complete a solo nonstop transatlantic flight in May 1932. She soloed in 1921, established an early women's altitude record of 14,000 feet in 1922, and later achieved feats including the first solo nonstop flight from Hawaii to the U.S. mainland in 1935. Earhart also promoted aviation through writing, public speaking, and fashion design aimed at active women, while serving as a career counselor at Purdue University. Her 1937 attempt to circumnavigate the globe equatorially in a Lockheed Electra, navigating with Fred Noonan, ended when the pair vanished over the Pacific Ocean en route to Howland Island after departing Lae, New Guinea; despite extensive searches, no definitive trace of Earhart, Noonan, or the aircraft has been confirmed, rendering the incident aviation 's most enduring unsolved mystery.
